summary: Existing MCP filesystem servers lack proper sandboxing — string-based path comparison, no symlink escape handling, no clear read/write permission model. MCP clients need controlled, auditable filesystem access.

text: MCP protocol compatibility over stdio transport using rmcp and Tokio
Strict filesystem sandboxing with canonical path comparison against allowed roots
Recursive allowed-root behavior — registering /Volumes/Data grants access to all descendants
Clear read/write/destructive tool semantics with per-root readOnly/readWrite modes
Single-binary distribution via cargo build --release
Strong test coverage for path escape, symlink behavior, readonly roots, and overlapping roots
Stdio MCP transport with rmcp crate

13 MCP tools: list_allowed_directories, read_text_file, read_media_file, read_multiple_files, write_file, edit_file, create_directory, list_directory, list_directory_with_sizes, directory_tree, move_file, search_files, get_file_info
Recursive sandbox with canonical path comparison (std::path::Path, not strings)
Per-root readOnly/readWrite access modes with most-specific-root-wins for overlaps
Symlink escape prevention via std::fs::canonicalize
JSON config file, CLI with --root and --config
Structured MCP error responses with error codes
Comprehensive test suite (sandbox, symlinks, readonly, overlapping, tool contracts)
HTTP/SSE transport (deferred)
Arbitrary command execution
File watching / change notification
Backup, sync, or versioning
Windows-specific path handling (v1: macOS and Linux only)
Recursive enumeration in list_allowed_directories
All path comparisons must use std::path::Path, never raw strings
Canonicalization via std::fs::canonicalize resolves symlinks and .. components
Blocking FS ops run on tokio::task::spawn_blocking
No unsafe blocks without explicit documentation and justification
Default maxReadBytes=10MiB, maxDirectoryEntries=10000, maxSearchResults=1000
rmcp crate provides sufficient MCP protocol support for stdio transport and tool registration
Tokio spawn_blocking is adequate for filesystem operations
std::fs::canonicalize resolves symlinks correctly on macOS and Linux
macOS and Linux path semantics are sufficiently similar for v1
